• Approximately [MATH: 68\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 1] standard deviation of the mean. This means that the area under the bell curve from [MATH: \mu-\sigma] to [MATH: \mu+\sigma] represents approximately [MATH: 68\%] of the total area under the curve (which equals [MATH: 1]).

    In other words, [MATH: P(\mu-\sigma \lt X \lt \mu + \sigma) \approx 0.68.]

  • Approximately [MATH: 95\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 2] standard deviations of the mean. This means that the area under the bell curve from [MATH: \mu-2\sigma] to [MATH: \mu+2\sigma] represents approximately [MATH: 95\%] of the total area under the curve.

    In other words, [MATH: P(\mu - 3\sigma \lt X \lt \mu + 3\sigma) \approx 0.997.]

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: X\sim N(\mu, \sigma)] is a normally distributed random variable. As we've seen, probabilities associated with [MATH: X] are often found using tables. However, there are cases where we can estimate probabilities associated with [MATH: X] without tables.

Content:
In particular, we have the following facts, applicable to all normally distributed random variables:

Content:
- Approximately [MATH: 68\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 1] standard deviation of the mean. This means that the area under the bell curve from [MATH: \mu-\sigma] to [MATH: \mu+\sigma] represents approximately [MATH: 68\%] of the total area under the curve (which equals [MATH: 1]).

[IMG: /graphics/438494c7848bf526b62abcb5f9859cdc]

In other words, [MATH: P(\mu-\sigma \lt X \lt \mu + \sigma) \approx 0.68.]
- Approximately [MATH: 95\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 2] standard deviations of the mean. This means that the area under the bell curve from [MATH: \mu-2\sigma] to [MATH: \mu+2\sigma] represents approximately [MATH: 95\%] of the total area under the curve.

[IMG: /graphics/cca618cd8580fe4affafb5c2323f792d]

In other words, [MATH: P(\mu - 2\sigma \lt X \lt \mu + 2\sigma) \approx 0.95.]
- Approximately [MATH: 99.7\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 3] standard deviations of the mean. This means that the area under the bell curve from [MATH: \mu-3\sigma] to [MATH: \mu+3\sigma] represents approximately [MATH: 99.7\%] of the total area under the curve.

[IMG: /graphics/0164e3c5d78a4746bf3880cddb56df8f]

In other words, [MATH: P(\mu - 3\sigma \lt X \lt \mu + 3\sigma) \approx 0.997.]
- Finally, approximately [MATH: 100\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 4] (or more) standard deviations of the mean. This means that the area under the bell curve from [MATH: \mu-k\sigma] to [MATH: \mu+k\sigma] for [MATH: k \geq 4] (almost) equals the total area under the curve.

In other words, if [MATH: k \geq 4,] then [MATH: P(\mu - k\sigma \lt X \lt \mu + k\sigma) \approx 1.]

sections.normalized_html: Given a normal distribution with a mean of [MATH: 18] and a variance of [MATH: 49,] use the empirical rule to estimate the percentage of the data points that are less than [MATH: 18] or greater than [MATH: 32.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since [MATH: \mu=18] and [MATH: \sigma=\sqrt{49} = 7,] we have the normal distribution shown below.

According to the empirical rule, we have the following:

  • Approximately [MATH: 68\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 1] standard deviation of the mean.

  • Approximately [MATH: 95\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 2] standard deviations of the mean.

  • Approximately [MATH: 99.7\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 3] standard deviations of the mean.

We can assume that [MATH: 100\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 4] (or more) standard deviations of the mean.

Now, notice that

  • [MATH: x=18] equals the mean: [MATH: \mu = 18]

  • [MATH: x=32] is [MATH: 2] standard deviations above the mean: [MATH: 32 = 18 + 2 \cdot 7 = \mu +2 \sigma]

The required percentage is represented by the area shown below.

From the diagram, the required percentage is

[MATH: 50\% + 2.35\%+0.15\%= 52.5\%.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: X\sim N(\mu, \sigma)] is a normally distributed random variable. As we've seen, probabilities associated with [MATH: X] are often found using tables. However, there are cases where we can estimate probabilities associated with [MATH: X] without tables.

Content:
In particular, we have the following facts, applicable to all normally distributed random variables:

Content:
- Approximately [MATH: 68\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 1] standard deviation of the mean. This means that the area under the bell curve from [MATH: \mu-\sigma] to [MATH: \mu+\sigma] represents approximately [MATH: 68\%] of the total area under the curve (which equals [MATH: 1]).

[IMG: /graphics/438494c7848bf526b62abcb5f9859cdc]

In other words, [MATH: P(\mu-\sigma \lt X \lt \mu + \sigma) \approx 0.68.]
- Approximately [MATH: 95\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 2] standard deviations of the mean. This means that the area under the bell curve from [MATH: \mu-2\sigma] to [MATH: \mu+2\sigma] represents approximately [MATH: 95\%] of the total area under the curve.

[IMG: /graphics/cca618cd8580fe4affafb5c2323f792d]

In other words, [MATH: P(\mu - 2\sigma \lt X \lt \mu + 2\sigma) \approx 0.95.]
- Approximately [MATH: 99.7\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 3] standard deviations of the mean. This means that the area under the bell curve from [MATH: \mu-3\sigma] to [MATH: \mu+3\sigma] represents approximately [MATH: 99.7\%] of the total area under the curve.

[IMG: /graphics/0164e3c5d78a4746bf3880cddb56df8f]

In other words, [MATH: P(\mu - 3\sigma \lt X \lt \mu + 3\sigma) \approx 0.997.]
- Finally, approximately [MATH: 100\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 4] (or more) standard deviations of the mean. This means that the area under the bell curve from [MATH: \mu-k\sigma] to [MATH: \mu+k\sigma] for [MATH: k \geq 4] (almost) equals the total area under the curve.

In other words, if [MATH: k \geq 4,] then [MATH: P(\mu - k\sigma \lt X \lt \mu + k\sigma) \approx 1.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Empirical Rule

Content:
Since the bell curve is symmetrical over the [MATH: y]-axis, all of the cases we just described can be summarized in one diagram.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/111fc26565714649c0dbfcc8749e7240]

Content:
Estimating the probabilities using this mnemonic diagram is called the empirical rule.

Content:
Notice that that empirical rule gives an approximate probability for each band of width [MATH: \sigma] (one standard deviation) from the mean [MATH: \mu.]

---

Item 3 — Example: Finding a Population Percentage Using the Empirical Rule

Example Prompt:
Given a normal distribution with a mean of [MATH: 18] and a variance of [MATH: 49,] use the empirical rule to estimate the percentage of the data points that are less than [MATH: 18] or greater than [MATH: 32.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since [MATH: \mu=18] and [MATH: \sigma=\sqrt{49} = 7,] we have the normal distribution shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/f6b56f534ea76283b6bbbfa06a97e2b1]

According to the empirical rule, we have the following:

- Approximately [MATH: 68\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 1] standard deviation of the mean.
- Approximately [MATH: 95\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 2] standard deviations of the mean.
- Approximately [MATH: 99.7\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 3] standard deviations of the mean.

We can assume that [MATH: 100\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 4] (or more) standard deviations of the mean.

Now, notice that

- [MATH: x=18] equals the mean:
[MATH: \mu = 18]
- [MATH: x=32] is [MATH: 2] standard deviations above the mean:
[MATH: 32 = 18 + 2 \cdot 7 = \mu +2 \sigma]

The required percentage is represented by the area shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/4172a3127cf874cb0f2d3e14b33573df]

From the diagram, the required percentage is

[MATH: 50\% + 2.35\%+0.15\%= 52.5\%.]

---

Item 6 — Example: Finding a Population Percentage in Context Using the Empirical Rule

Example Prompt:
A particular organization only admits members with an IQ of at least [MATH: 130.] It's known that IQ is normally distributed with a mean of [MATH: 100] and a variance of [MATH: 225.] Use the empirical rule to estimate the percentage of people in the general population that would not be admitted to this organization.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since [MATH: \mu=100] and [MATH: \sigma=\sqrt {225} = 15,] we have the normal distribution shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/ae5b1934f33eb54e6bfd0402a55395e5]

According to the empirical rule, we have the following:

- Approximately [MATH: 68\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 1] standard deviation of the mean.
- Approximately [MATH: 95\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 2] standard deviations of the mean.
- Approximately [MATH: 99.7\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 3] standard deviations of the mean.

We can assume that [MATH: 100\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 4] (or more) standard deviations of the mean.

Now, notice that [MATH: x=130] is [MATH: 2] standard deviations above the mean:
[MATH: 130 = 100 + 2 \cdot 15 = \mu +2 \sigma]

We are interested only in those with an IQ of less than [MATH: 130.] The required percentage is represented by the area shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/2fe34d059365e7b31c4a5507148dd319]

From the diagram, the required percentage is

[MATH: 100\%-(2.35\% + 0.15\%) = 97.5 \%]

---

Item 9 — Tutorial: Estimators and Estimates

Content:
Suppose a population is normally distributed with known mean [MATH: \mu] and unknown variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] We can use empirical data to estimate the variance.

Content:
For example, let's assume our normal population has mean [MATH: \mu = 12] and unknown variance. Suppose an independent random sample is drawn from the population, and it is found that approximately [MATH: 68\%] of the data in the sample have a value between [MATH: 7] and [MATH: 17.]

Content:
According to the empirical rule, we have the following:

Content:
- Approximately [MATH: 68\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 1] standard deviation of the mean.
- Approximately [MATH: 95\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 2] standard deviations of the mean.
- Approximately [MATH: 99.7\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 3] standard deviations of the mean.

Content:
We can assume that [MATH: 100\%] of the data falls within [MATH: 4] (or more) standard deviations of the mean.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9b9c2d8251ffa16ee68cfc9effa2ee2d]

Content:
So, according to this rule, [MATH: 68\%] of the observations of a random normal variable [MATH: N(\mu, \sigma^2)] fall in the interval [MATH: (\mu-\sigma, \mu+\sigma).] This range represents [MATH: 2] standard deviations. Therefore, we can write:

Content:
[MATH: μ − σ^(^)|= 7; μ + σ^(^)|= 17]

Content:
We have used [MATH: \widehat{\sigma}] since the sample data will give an estimate of the population standard deviation [MATH: \sigma.] Since the observations used to formulate these equations came from sample data, we cannot assume that [MATH: \widehat{\sigma} = \sigma.] However, if the sample is large, [MATH: \widehat{\sigma}] should give a reasonable approximation to [MATH: \sigma.]

Content:
We wish to solve for [MATH: \widehat{\sigma}.] First, we subtract the first equation from the second, which gives
[MATH: 2\widehat{\sigma} = 17-7 = 10.]
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\sigma} = \dfrac{10}{2} = 5.]

Content:
Finally, the estimate of the population variance is given by
[MATH: \widehat{\sigma}^2 = 5^2 = 25.]

---
